summary: North Korea (the Democratic People's Republic of Korea) is located in the northern part of the Korean Peninsula; founded in 1948 and ruled by the Kim family, it is one of the most isolated countries in the world.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: After the Soviet Union occupied northern Korea in 1945 and Kim Il Sung founded the Democratic People's Republic of Korea in 1948, the government promoted Marxism–Leninism and atheism; in the 1950s it confiscated religious property and persecuted religious people, and large numbers of Christians and religious figures fled south or were executed. From the 1970s the Juche idea became the official ideology, and the worship of the Kim Il Sung family took the place of religion. Although the constitution nominally guarantees freedom of belief, in practice religious activity is strictly controlled, and most people are classified as non-religious.

ranking.name: Shamanism
ranking.description: Shamanism (musok) is the oldest religious tradition on the Korean Peninsula, in which shamans (mudang) conduct rites to communicate with spirits and ancestors. The North Korean government regards it as superstition and bans it, but according to the testimony of defectors, divination and folk rites seeking safety and well-being spread privately among the people in times of economic hardship, especially after the great famine of the 'Arduous March' in the 1990s, so a certain proportion of people are estimated to still hold shamanistic beliefs.

ranking.name: Cheondoism
ranking.description: Cheondoism originated from Donghak, founded by Choe Je-u in 1860, which blends Confucianism, Buddhism, Daoism and folk beliefs and holds that 'man is Heaven'. Cheondoists took part in both the Donghak Peasant Revolution of 1894 and the March 1st Independence Movement of 1919, and were deeply influential among farmers in the north. The North Korean government still keeps the 'Chondoist Chongu Party' as a token party of the united front, so Cheondoism is the only indigenous religion with some standing within the official structure.

ranking.name: Buddhism
ranking.description: Buddhism was introduced from China in the 4th century during the Goguryeo period and became the state religion during the Goryeo dynasty, leaving many temples around Kaesong. The Joseon dynasty promoted Confucianism and suppressed Buddhism, and Buddhism gradually declined. After the founding of North Korea most temples were converted into cultural heritage sites, managed by the official Korean Buddhist Federation, and temples such as Pohyon Temple on Mount Myohyang serve mainly as tourist attractions, with few believers.

ranking.name: Christianity
ranking.description: Christianity was introduced in the late 19th century by American Presbyterians, and Pyongyang was called the 'Jerusalem of the East' because of the Great Revival of 1907, being the center of Christianity on the Korean Peninsula. After 1945 the North Korean government carried out large-scale persecution of Christians, and hundreds of thousands fled south. Although Pyongyang has several official churches today, private believers who are discovered are severely punished, and the proportion of Christians is extremely low.

religion.background: Shamanism has existed in the northern Korean Peninsula since ancient times; Buddhism came from China in the 4th century, and during the Joseon dynasty Confucianism was dominant. In the late 19th century Christianity and Donghak (Cheondoism) rose in the north, and Pyongyang became a center of Christianity. After 1945 North Korea established a communist regime with Soviet support, promoted atheism and persecuted religion, and the Juche idea and the cult of the leader took the place of religion. The authorities keep a few religious organizations for foreign propaganda, but actual religious freedom is extremely limited.

ranking.name: Korean
ranking.description: Korean is the language of the Korean Peninsula; in 1443 King Sejong of Joseon created Hunminjeongeum (the Hangul alphabet), enabling commoners to read and write as well. North Korea abolished Chinese characters in 1949 and uses Hangul exclusively; in 1966 Kim Il Sung put forward the 'Cultured Language' policy, taking the Pyongyang dialect as the standard and replacing many Sino-Korean words and loanwords with native words. Because the population is almost entirely ethnic Korean and isolated from the outside world, Korean is the only language used across the country. After more than seventy years of division between North and South, the vocabulary and pronunciation of the two have shown clear differences.

language.history: Korean was written in Chinese characters from ancient times, and in 1443 King Sejong created Hunminjeongeum. In the later part of Japanese colonial rule (1910–1945), Japanese-language education was promoted and Korean was restricted. After the division in 1945, North Korea abolished Chinese characters in 1949, and in 1966 promoted the 'Cultured Language' based on the Pyongyang dialect, carrying out language purification and replacing many Sino-Korean words and loanwords. South Korea, by contrast, takes the Seoul dialect as its standard language, and the languages of the two gradually diverged.

ranking.name: Pyongyang naengmyeon (cold noodles)
ranking.description: Long thin noodles made mainly from buckwheat are placed in an ice-cold, clear beef broth or in a northeastern-style dongchimi (radish water kimchi) broth, topped with sliced beef, Asian pear, cucumber and a boiled egg, with a light, refreshing taste.
ranking.history: Pyongyang naengmyeon was a local dish of Pyeongan Province in the Joseon dynasty; in the cold mountainous north, buckwheat is easier to grow than rice. Traditionally it was a dish eaten in winter on warm ondol floors. Okryugwan in Pyongyang, founded in 1960, is North Korea's most famous naengmyeon restaurant. During the Korean War, large numbers of northern refugees moved south and brought Pyongyang naengmyeon to Seoul; at the 2018 inter-Korean summit, North Korea specially brought chefs and a noodle-making machine from Okryugwan to Panmunjom, and naengmyeon thus became a symbol of inter-Korean exchange.

ranking.name: Kimchi
ranking.description: Napa cabbage, radish and other vegetables are salted, then coated with seasonings such as chili powder, garlic, ginger and fish sauce and fermented, giving a sour, spicy and savory taste. North Korean kimchi is usually milder in spiciness than South Korean kimchi.
ranking.history: The history of pickled vegetables on the Korean Peninsula can be traced back to the Three Kingdoms period, but chili pepper was added only after it was introduced via Japan around the 17th century, producing today's red kimchi. Every early winter, households together pickle large quantities of kimchi for the winter, called 'kimjang'. In 2015 UNESCO inscribed North Korea's 'Tradition of kimchi-making' on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, after South Korea's kimjang culture was inscribed in 2013.

ranking.name: Bindaetteok (mung bean pancake)
ranking.description: Soaked mung beans are ground into a batter, mixed with bean sprouts, kimchi, pork and scallions, and fried in oil in a pan into a thick round pancake, crispy outside and soft inside.
ranking.history: Bindaetteok is a local dish of Pyeongan Province, and Pyongyang's version is known for being thick and rich in the aroma of lard. There are various theories about the name, one of which holds that it was once food given out to the poor. In the Joseon dynasty it was one of the dishes placed on the altar during ancestral rites, and today it is still common at festivals and family gatherings in North Korea, and is also a side dish for Pyongyang onban.

ranking.name: Onban (Pyongyang warm rice)
ranking.description: White rice is topped with shredded chicken, bindaetteok and shiitake mushrooms, then drenched in hot chicken broth; light and warming, it is a representative local dish of Pyongyang.
ranking.history: Onban is a traditional Pyongyang dish whose name means 'warm rice', and it is especially popular in the cold northern winters. Because chicken broth and rice were both precious ingredients in the past, onban was often used to entertain guests or eaten on festive occasions, and old established restaurants in Pyongyang still make it their signature dish today. It is one of Pyongyang's representative local dishes, commonly seen at festivals and when entertaining guests.

ranking.name: Mandu (dumplings)
ranking.description: Dough wrappers are filled with a mixture of pork, tofu, kimchi and vegetables, and can be steamed, boiled or fried; northern mandu are usually larger.
ranking.history: Mandu is generally thought to have been introduced to the Korean Peninsula from the Yuan dynasty via the Mongols in the 14th century, at the end of the Goryeo dynasty, and the name shares its origin with the Chinese 'mantou'. Because the north is cold and has more wheat and buckwheat, mandu are especially popular in northern Korea, and traditionally mandu soup is cooked at Lunar New Year, symbolizing the addition of a year of age. During the Korean War, northern refugees moving south also brought northern mandu to South Korea.
